claim: Subcortical structures play a role in high-level cognitive functions such as the allocation of spatial attention.
source: Evidence suggests that subcortical structures play a role in high-level cognitive functions such as the allocation of spatial attention.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to existing literature as indicated by the general statement in the abstract.

claim: Posterior alpha band oscillations are modulated by spatial attention in humans.
source: While there is abundant evidence in humans for posterior alpha band oscillations being modulated by spatial attention, little is known about how subcortical regions contribute to these oscillatory modulations, particularly under varying conditions of cognitive challenge.
evidence: The claim references abundant evidence, indicating support from existing literature.

claim: Lateral asymmetry of the globus pallidus, caudate nucleus, and thalamus predicted attention-related modulations of posterior alpha oscillations.
source: Lateral asymmetry of the globus pallidus, caudate nucleus, and thalamus predicted attention-related modulations of posterior alpha oscillations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis combining MEG and MRI data.

claim: When the perceptual load was applied to the target and the distractor was salient, caudate nucleus asymmetry predicted alpha-band modulations.
source: When the perceptual load was applied to the target and the distractor was salient caudate nucleus asymmetry predicted alpha-band modulations.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's analysis of different load conditions.

claim: Globus pallidus was predictive of alpha-band modulations when either the target had a high load, or the distractor was salient, but not both.
source: Globus pallidus was predictive of alpha-band modulations when either the target had a high load, or the distractor was salient, but not both.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's analysis of different load conditions.

claim: The asymmetry of the thalamus predicted alpha band modulation when neither component of the task was perceptually demanding.
source: Finally, the asymmetry of the thalamus predicted alpha band modulation when neither component of the task was perceptually demanding.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's analysis of different load conditions.

claim: The dorsal attention network consists of the intraparietal sulcus/superior parietal lobule, and the frontal eye fields.
source: The dorsal attention network, which consists of the intraparietal sulcus/superior parietal lobule, and the frontal eye fields, is the most predominant network associated with the allocation of attention (Kastner et al., 1999; Hopfinger et al., 2000; Corbetta et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kastner et al., 1999; Hopfinger et al., 2000; Corbetta et al., 2000.

claim: The dorsal attention network is the most predominant network associated with the allocation of attention.
source: The dorsal attention network, which consists of the intraparietal sulcus/superior parietal lobule, and the frontal eye fields, is the most predominant network associated with the allocation of attention (Kastner et al., 1999; Hopfinger et al., 2000; Corbetta et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kastner et al., 1999; Hopfinger et al., 2000; Corbetta et al., 2000.

claim: MEG and EEG are not well suited for detecting subcortical activity.
source: One reason, amongst many others, is that MEG and EEG are not well suited for detecting subcortical activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The pulvinar plays an important role in the modulation of neocortical alpha oscillations associated with the allocation of attention.
source: For instance, it has been shown that the pulvinar plays an important role in the modulation of neocortical alpha oscillations associated with the allocation of attention (Kastner et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kastner et al., 2020.

claim: Both the thalamus and superior colliculus are involved in the control of spatial attention by contributing to the regulation of neocortical activity.
source: Studies in rats and non-human primates have shown that both the thalamus and superior colliculus, are involved in the control of spatial attention by contributing to the regulation of neocortical activity (Kastner et al., 2020; Krauzlis et al., 2013; Krauzlis et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kastner et al., 2020; Krauzlis et al., 2013; Krauzlis et al., 2018.

claim: When the pulvinar was inactivated after muscimol infusion, the monkey's ability to detect color changes in attended stimuli was lowered.
source: Notably, when the largest nucleus of the thalamus, the pulvinar, was inactivated after muscimol infusion, the monkey's ability to detect color changes in attended stimuli was lowered. This behavioral deficit occurred when the target was in the receptive field of V4 neurons that were connected to lesioned pulvinar (Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: The basal ganglia play a role in different aspects of cognitive control, encompassing attention, behavioural output, and conscious perception.
source: The basal ganglia play a role in different aspects of cognitive control, encompassing attention (van Schouwenburg et al., 2010; Nakajima et al., 2019), behavioural output (Moolchand et al., 2022), and conscious perception (Slagter et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to van Schouwenburg et al., 2010; Nakajima et al., 2019; Moolchand et al., 2022; Slagter et al., 2017.

claim: The basal ganglia contribute to visuospatial attention by linking with cortical regions like the prefrontal cortex via the thalamus.
source: Moreover, the basal ganglia contribute to visuospatial attention by linking with cortical regions like the prefrontal cortex via the thalamus.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on anatomical tracing studies mentioned in the following sentence.

claim: Anatomical tracing studies on selective attention and distractor suppression point to a key role of prefrontal-basal ganglia-thalamus pathway whereby sensory thalamic activity is regulated by prefrontal cortex via basal ganglia.
source: Anatomical tracing studies on selective attention and distractor suppression point to a key role of prefrontal-basal ganglia-thalamus pathway whereby sensory thalamic activity is regulated by prefrontal cortex via basal ganglia (Nakajima et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nakajima et al., 2019.

claim: fMRI studies in humans demonstrated increased activation in basal ganglia when covert attention was reallocated.
source: Furthermore, fMRI studies in humans demonstrated increased activation in basal ganglia when covert attention was reallocated.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from fMRI studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Dynamic causal modelling has shown that the basal ganglia can modulate the top-down influence of the prefrontal cortex on the visual cortex in a task-dependent manner.
source: Additionally, dynamic causal modelling has shown that the basal ganglia can modulate the top-down influence of the prefrontal cortex on the visual cortex in a task-dependent manner (van Schouwenburg et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to van Schouwenburg et al., 2015.

claim: Power modulation of oscillatory activity in the alpha band (8–13 Hz) has been proposed to reflect resource allocation between goal-relevant and irrelevant stimuli.
source: In terms of neuronal dynamics, power modulation of oscillatory activity in the alpha band (8–13 Hz) has been proposed to reflect resource allocation between goal-relevant and irrelevant stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as an established proposal in the field.

claim: Studies in EEG and MEG typically find an alpha power decrease in the hemisphere contralateral to the attended stimuli complemented by a relative increase in alpha power in the other hemisphere associated with unattended stimuli.
source: Such studies typically find an alpha power decrease in the hemisphere contralateral to the attended stimuli complemented by a relative increase in alpha power in the other hemisphere associated with unattended stimuli (Okazaki et al., 2014; Thut et al., 2006; Worden et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Okazaki et al., 2014; Thut et al., 2006; Worden et al., 2000.

claim: When the target stimulus has a higher perceptual load, alpha band power increases in ipsilateral regions thus indirectly reflecting distractor suppression.
source: Indeed, a recent study demonstrated when the target stimulus has a higher perceptual load (e.g. more difficult to perceive), alpha band power increases in ipsilateral regions thus indirectly reflecting distractor suppression (Gutteling et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gutteling et al., 2022.

claim: The hemispheric lateralized modulation of alpha oscillations is correlated with the volumetric hemispheric asymmetry of both the globus pallidus and the thalamus.
source: Using this approach, it was shown that the hemispheric lateralized modulation of alpha oscillations is correlated with the volumetric hemispheric asymmetry of both the globus pallidus and the thalamus (Mazzetti et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mazzetti et al., 2019.

claim: The relationship between the globus pallidus and the modulation of alpha oscillations was demonstrated in the trials where the visual stimuli were associated with high-value (positive or negative) reward valence.
source: The relationship between the globus pallidus and the modulation of alpha oscillations was demonstrated in the trials where the visual stimuli were associated with high-value (positive or negative) reward valence.
evidence: This refers to findings from Mazzetti et al., 2019 mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: A power decrease contralateral to the cued hemifield and a relative increase ipsilaterally was observed.
source: As expected from a previous report (Gutteling et al., 2022), we observed a power decrease contralateral to the cued hemifield and a relative increase ipsilaterally (i.e. an increase contralateral to the distractor, Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Gutteling et al., 2022.

claim: The magnitude of the modulation index (MI(α)) reflecting the relative difference in alpha power when attending left versus right, gradually decreased and increased over respectively the left and right hemisphere until target onset.
source: As expected, the magnitude of the modulation index (MI(α)) reflecting the relative difference in alpha power when attending left versus right, gradually decreased and increased over respectively the left and right hemisphere until target onset (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HLM(α) indices range from ~–0.15 to 0.15 and are normally distributed around zero before target onset.
source: HLM(α) indices range from ~–0.15 to 0.15 and are normally distributed around zero before target onset (Shapiro-Wilk, W=0.966, p-value = 0.3895).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results (Shapiro-Wilk test).

claim: Caudate nucleus was right lateralized.
source: We found that caudate nucleus was right lateralized (p-value = 0.021), whereas, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and thalamus volumes showed left lateralization (p-value = 0.004, p-value <0.001 and p-value <0.001, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of volumetric data with p-value = 0.021.

claim: Putamen, nucleus accumbens, and thalamus volumes showed left lateralization.
source: We found that caudate nucleus was right lateralized (p-value = 0.021), whereas, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and thalamus volumes showed left lateralization (p-value = 0.004, p-value <0.001 and p-value <0.001, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of volumetric data with respective p-values.

claim: Thalamus has significantly negative LV values (i.e. left lateralization) with mean ± std = –0.0123±0.0121, p-value <0.000.
source: Thalamus (mean ± std = –0.0123±0.0121, p-value <0.000), putamen (mean ± std = –0.0149±0.0285, p-value = 0.004) and nucleus accumbens (mean ± std = –0.1141±0.0746, p-value <0.000) have significantly negative LV values (i.e. left lateralization) whereas the caudate nucleus is right lateralized (mean ± std = 0.0115±0.0285, p-value = 0.021; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with specific mean, standard deviation, and p-value, and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Putamen has significantly negative LV values (i.e. left lateralization) with mean ± std = –0.0149±0.0285, p-value = 0.004.
source: Thalamus (mean ± std = –0.0123±0.0121, p-value <0.000), putamen (mean ± std = –0.0149±0.0285, p-value = 0.004) and nucleus accumbens (mean ± std = –0.1141±0.0746, p-value <0.000) have significantly negative LV values (i.e. left lateralization) whereas the caudate nucleus is right lateralized (mean ± std = 0.0115±0.0285, p-value = 0.021; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with specific mean, standard deviation, and p-value, and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Nucleus accumbens has significantly negative LV values (i.e. left lateralization) with mean ± std = –0.1141±0.0746, p-value <0.000.
source: Thalamus (mean ± std = –0.0123±0.0121, p-value <0.000), putamen (mean ± std = –0.0149±0.0285, p-value = 0.004) and nucleus accumbens (mean ± std = –0.1141±0.0746, p-value <0.000) have significantly negative LV values (i.e. left lateralization) whereas the caudate nucleus is right lateralized (mean ± std = 0.0115±0.0285, p-value = 0.021; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with specific mean, standard deviation, and p-value, and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Caudate nucleus is right lateralized with mean ± std = 0.0115±0.0285, p-value = 0.021.
source: Thalamus (mean ± std = –0.0123±0.0121, p-value <0.000), putamen (mean ± std = –0.0149±0.0285, p-value = 0.004) and nucleus accumbens (mean ± std = –0.1141±0.0746, p-value <0.000) have significantly negative LV values (i.e. left lateralization) whereas the caudate nucleus is right lateralized (mean ± std = 0.0115±0.0285, p-value = 0.021; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis with specific mean, standard deviation, and p-value, and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Globus pallidus, hippocampus, and amygdala did not show any robust volume lateralization.
source: Globus pallidus, hippocampus, and amygdala did not show any robust volume lateralization.
evidence: This is a finding from the volumetric analysis of subcortical structures.

claim: Participants with larger volumes of the caudate nucleus in the left compared to the right hemisphere showed higher modulations in alpha power over the left compared to the right hemisphere (and vice versa).
source: The analysis showed that the participants with larger volumes of the caudate nucleus in the left compared to the right hemisphere showed higher modulations in alpha power over the left compared to the right hemisphere (and vice versa).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GLM results showing the relationship between caudate nucleus lateralization and alpha modulation.

claim: There was a trend for the same effect for the globus pallidus whereas the thalamus shows the opposite effect.
source: There was a trend for the same effect for the globus pallidus whereas the thalamus shows the opposite effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GLM results.

claim: The winning model contained LVTh (β = –2.19, T(29) = –2.74, se = 0.80, p=0.010), LVCN (β = 0.92, T(29) = 2.83, se = 0.33, p-value = 0.008) and LVGP (β = 0.51, T(29) = 1.95, se = 0.26, p-value = 0.061) as regressors.
source: These results were observed from the winning model that contained LVTh, (β = –2.19, T(29) = –2.74, se = 0.80, p=0.010), LVCN (β = 0.92, T(29) = 2.83, se = 0.33, p-value = 0.008) and LVGP (β = 0.51, T(29) = 1.95, se = 0.26, p-value = 0.061) as regressors.
evidence: These are the statistical results from the GLM analysis.

claim: This model predicted the HLM(α) values significantly in the GLM (F3,29 = 7.4824, p=0.0007, adjusted R2=0.376) as compared with an intercept-only null model.
source: This model predicted the HLM(α) values significantly in the GLM (F3,29 = 7.4824, p=0.0007, adjusted R2=0.376) as compared with an intercept-only null model (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is the result of the GLM analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both thalamus and caudate nucleus showed a significant linear partial regression with hemispheric lateralization modulation in the alpha band in the opposite and same direction.
source: These findings are illustrated in Figure 4B, confirming that both thalamus and caudate nucleus showed a significant linear partial regression with hemispheric lateralization modulation in the alpha band in the opposite and same direction.
evidence: This is confirmed by the partial regression plots in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Removing LVGP from the regression resulted in worse models.
source: Although, the β estimate of LVGP only showed a positive trend, removing it from the regression resulted in worse models (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on model comparison analysis shown in supplementary files.

claim: Neither the behavioural nor the rapid invisible frequency tagging (RIFT) measures showed significant relationships with LVs and HLM(α).
source: It is worth noting that neither the behavioural nor the rapid invisible frequency tagging (RIFT) measures showed significant relationships with LVs and HLM(α) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Comparison of the full and reduced models showed that the selected regressors predicted variability in HLM(α) values to an extent that was greater than chance (F(25,28) = 2.03, p-value = 0.037).
source: Comparison of the full (i.e. MMR including the LV values of all seven subcortical structures as regressors) and reduced (i.e. MMR with all structures excluding the selected structures) models showed that our selected regressors predicted variability in HLM(α) values to an extent that was greater than chance (F(25,28) = 2.03, p-value = 0.037).
evidence: This is the result of the multivariate multiple regression analysis.

claim: The MMR model was significantly different from the null model (F(29,31) = 3.78, p-value = 0.0015).
source: This was further confirmed when we compared the MMR model with the null model (i.e. MMR including only subject intercepts as regressor; F(29,31) = 3.78, p-value = 0.0015).
evidence: This is the result of comparing the MMR model to a null model.

claim: The thalamus had significant LV values in condition 1 (i.e. low-load target, non-salient distractor) with β = –3.63 (T(29) = –2.64, se = 1.37, p-value = 0.0132).
source: Our analysis, as shown in Figure 5, demonstrated that the thalamus had significant LV values in condition 1 (i.e. low-load target, non-salient distractor) with β = –3.63 (T(29) = –2.64, se = 1.37, p-value = 0.0132).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and is a result of the MMR analysis.

claim: Globus pallidus showed a significant β coefficient in conditions 2 (i.e., high-load target, non-salient distractor) with β = 0.93, (T(29) = 2.15, se = 0.43, p-value = 0.040).
source: Globus pallidus showed a significant β coefficient in conditions 2 (i.e., high-load target, non-salient distractor) and 3 (i.e. low-load target, salient distractor) with β = 0.93, (T(29) = 2.15, se = 0.43, p-value = 0.040) and β = 0.89 (T(29) = 2.30, se = 0.39, p-value = 0.029), respectively.
evidence: This is a result of the MMR analysis for different load conditions.

claim: Globus pallidus showed a significant β coefficient in conditions 3 (i.e. low-load target, salient distractor) with β = 0.89 (T(29) = 2.30, se = 0.39, p-value = 0.029).
source: Globus pallidus showed a significant β coefficient in conditions 2 (i.e., high-load target, non-salient distractor) and 3 (i.e. low-load target, salient distractor) with β = 0.93, (T(29) = 2.15, se = 0.43, p-value = 0.040) and β = 0.89 (T(29) = 2.30, se = 0.39, p-value = 0.029), respectively.
evidence: This is a result of the MMR analysis for different load conditions.

claim: Condition 4 (i.e. high-load target, salient distractor) was the only condition in which the caudate nucleus had a β estimate significantly different than zero (β = 1.64, T(29) = 2.07, se = 0.79, p-value = 0.049).
source: Condition 4 (i.e. high-load target, salient distractor) was the only condition in which the caudate nucleus had a β estimate significantly different than zero (β = 1.64, T(29) = 2.07, se = 0.79, p-value = 0.049).
evidence: This is a result of the MMR analysis for different load conditions.

claim: Caudate nucleus can predict variability across all four of the task conditions with marginal significancy (F(26,4) = 2.82, p-value = 0.046).
source: We found that while, with marginal significancy, caudate nucleus can predict variability across all four of the task conditions (F(26,4) = 2.82, p-value = 0.046), the predictive relationships of thalamus (F(26,4) = 2.43, p-value = 0.073) with condition 1, and globus pallidus (F(26,4) = 2.29, p-value = 0.087) with conditions 2 and 3 hold only for these conditions.
evidence: This is the result of statistical tests on the MMR results.

claim: The predictive relationships of thalamus (F(26,4) = 2.43, p-value = 0.073) with condition 1 hold only for this condition.
source: We found that while, with marginal significancy, caudate nucleus can predict variability across all four of the task conditions (F(26,4) = 2.82, p-value = 0.046), the predictive relationships of thalamus (F(26,4) = 2.43, p-value = 0.073) with condition 1, and globus pallidus (F(26,4) = 2.29, p-value = 0.087) with conditions 2 and 3 hold only for these conditions.
evidence: This is the result of statistical tests on the MMR results.

claim: The predictive relationships of globus pallidus (F(26,4) = 2.29, p-value = 0.087) with conditions 2 and 3 hold only for these conditions.
source: We found that while, with marginal significancy, caudate nucleus can predict variability across all four of the task conditions (F(26,4) = 2.82, p-value = 0.046), the predictive relationships of thalamus (F(26,4) = 2.43, p-value = 0.073) with condition 1, and globus pallidus (F(26,4) = 2.29, p-value = 0.087) with conditions 2 and 3 hold only for these conditions.
evidence: This is the result of statistical tests on the MMR results.

claim: When the task is easiest (condition 1), the thalamus is related to alpha modulation.
source: In sum, this demonstrates that when the task is easiest (condition 1), the thalamus is related to alpha modulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MMR results.

claim: When the task is most difficult (condition 4), the caudate nucleus relates to the alpha modulation.
source: When the task is most difficult (condition 4), the caudate nucleus relates to the alpha modulation; however, its contributions are substantial enough to predict outcomes across all conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MMR results.

claim: For the conditions with medium difficulty (conditions 2 and 3), the globus pallidus is related to the alpha band modulation.
source: For the conditions with medium difficulty (conditions 2 and 3), the globus pallidus is related to the alpha band modulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MMR results.

claim: Extensive navigation experience enlarges the size of right hippocampus.
source: It has been demonstrated that extensive navigation experience enlarges the size of right hippocampus (Maguire et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maguire et al., 2000.

claim: In Parkinson's disease, atrophy in the nucleus accumbens and thalamus correlated with cognitive impairments.
source: In Parkinson's disease, atrophy in the nucleus accumbens and thalamus correlated with cognitive impairments (Mak et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mak et al., 2014.

claim: Patients with Alzheimer's Disease have been shown to have a significantly smaller amygdala, thalamus, caudate nucleus, putamen, and nucleus accumbens than matched controls.
source: In a large-scale study on 773 participants, patients with Alzheimer's Disease have been shown to have a significantly smaller amygdala, thalamus, caudate nucleus, putamen, and nucleus accumbens than matched controls (Yi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yi et al., 2016.

claim: The spatial extent of pathological change in subcortical structures can predict cognitive changes in Parkinson's Disease.
source: It has also been shown that the spatial extent of pathological change in subcortical structures can predict cognitive changes in Parkinson's Disease (Ye et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ye et al., 2022.

claim: Patients with symptomatic Huntington's Disease show significantly smaller caudate nucleus than pre-symptomatic participants who were carriers of Huntington's Disease gene mutation.
source: Patients with symptomatic Huntington's Disease also show significantly smaller caudate nucleus than pre-symptomatic participants who were carriers of Huntington's Disease gene mutation (Aylward et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aylward et al., 2000.

claim: Individuals with Alzheimer's Disease demonstrate an increase in slow oscillatory activities and a decrease in higher frequency oscillations.
source: For example, individuals with Alzheimer's Disease demonstrate an increase in slow oscillatory activities and a decrease in higher frequency oscillations (Jafari et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jafari et al., 2020.

claim: In patients with Parkinson's Disease, the power of beta oscillations increases relatively to when they are dopamine-depleted compared with when they are on dopaminergic medication.
source: Moreover, in patients with Parkinson's Disease, the power of beta oscillations increases relatively to when they are dopamine-depleted compared with when they are on dopaminergic medication (Jenkinson and Brown, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jenkinson and Brown, 2011.

claim: The volume of basal ganglia relates to the ability to modulate posterior brain oscillations in attention type tasks.
source: Based on these considerations, we argue that the volume of basal ganglia relates to the ability to modulate posterior brain oscillations in attention type tasks.
evidence: This is an argument based on the considerations from previous literature and the current study's approach.

claim: The pulvinar supports the allocation of spatial attention by driving the oscillatory synchrony in the alpha band between cortical areas in a task-dependent manner.
source: For example, the largest nucleus of the thalamus, the pulvinar, supports the allocation of spatial attention by driving the oscillatory synchrony in the alpha band between cortical areas in a task-dependent manner (Saalmann et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Saalmann et al., 2012.

claim: The caudate nucleus is involved in the allocation of spatial attention.
source: Also, our finding are consistent with other studies suggestions a role for the caudate nucleus (Bogadhi et al., 2018) and the pulvinar when allocating spatial attention (Bogadhi et al., 2018; Green et al., 2017; Petersen et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bogadhi et al., 2018.

claim: The pulvinar is involved in allocating spatial attention.
source: Also, our finding are consistent with other studies suggestions a role for the caudate nucleus (Bogadhi et al., 2018) and the pulvinar when allocating spatial attention (Bogadhi et al., 2018; Green et al., 2017; Petersen et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bogadhi et al., 2018; Green et al., 2017; Petersen et al., 1987.

claim: Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus has been shown to suppress oscillatory activity in the alpha and beta (8–22 Hz) frequency bands.
source: Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus has been shown to suppress oscillatory activity in the alpha and beta (8–22 Hz) frequency bands (Abbasi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Abbasi et al., 2018.

claim: The regression analysis outcomes align with the findings of Mazzetti et al., 2019 underscoring the significant predictive influence exerted by the lateralized volume of globus pallidus on the modulation of hemispheric lateralization in alpha oscillations during spatial attention tasks.
source: Furthermore, our regression analysis outcomes align with the findings of Mazzetti et al., 2019 underscoring the significant predictive influence exerted by the lateralized volume of globus pallidus on the modulation of hemispheric lateralization in alpha oscillations during spatial attention tasks.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's findings with Mazzetti et al., 2019.

claim: The thalamus plays a role in relaying information between the basal ganglia and the prefrontal cortex.
source: Involvement of the thalamus when the task is in its simplest form can be explained by its role relaying information between the basal ganglia and the prefrontal cortex (McFarland and Haber, 2002; Jeon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McFarland and Haber, 2002; Jeon et al., 2014.

claim: The globus pallidus contains GABAergic interneurons.
source: The opposite effect of the globus pallidus compared to the thalamus is striking, and possibly explained by the globus pallidus containing GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the globus pallidus.

claim: The inhibitory nature of the globus pallidus projections to thalamus could explain why they are related to the alpha modulation in different manners.
source: Thus the inhibitory nature of the globus pallidus projections to thalamus could explain why they are related to the alpha modulation in different manners (Lanciego et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Lanciego et al., 2012.

claim: Activation of caudate nucleus occurs only in the higher level cognitive hierarchy in a working memory selection task.
source: The involvement of the caudate nucleus in the most difficult condition is also in line with previous findings showing activation of caudate nucleus only in the higher level cognitive hierarchy in a working memory selection (Chatham et al., 2014) as well as a language task (Jeon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chatham et al., 2014.

claim: Activation of caudate nucleus occurs in higher level cognitive hierarchy in a language task.
source: The involvement of the caudate nucleus in the most difficult condition is also in line with previous findings showing activation of caudate nucleus only in the higher level cognitive hierarchy in a working memory selection (Chatham et al., 2014) as well as a language task (Jeon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jeon et al., 2014.

claim: Globus pallidus has a central role in harmonizing firing rates across the cortico-basal-ganglia circuits.
source: The engagement of globus pallidus might be reflected from its central role in harmonizing firing rates across the cortico-basal-ganglia circuits (Crompe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Crompe et al., 2020.

claim: Globus pallidus has wide projections to the thalamus.
source: Globus pallidus also has wide projections to the thalamus (Goldberg et al., 2013) and can thereby impact the dorsal attentional networks by modulating prefrontal activities (Nakajima et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Goldberg et al., 2013.

claim: Globus pallidus can impact the dorsal attentional networks by modulating prefrontal activities.
source: Globus pallidus also has wide projections to the thalamus (Goldberg et al., 2013) and can thereby impact the dorsal attentional networks by modulating prefrontal activities (Nakajima et al., 2019).
